name: Ruhollah Khomeini
description: Iranian revolutionary leader assessed through clerical state authority, social restrictions and the early Islamic Republic’s mixed economy.

axes.brief: Guardianship of the jurist, candidate restrictions and suppression of secular opposition subordinated elected bodies to clerical authority.
axes.counter: Referendums and elected institutions existed within restricted boundaries; the supreme leader’s religious authority was not identical to rule by armed forces or trade unions.

axes.brief: Religious moral enforcement, censorship, revolutionary courts and detention sharply limited individual liberties.
axes.counter: Voluntary private activity and some formal procedures persisted; exact contemporary data and internet rules remain historical analogies.

axes.brief: A shared Islamic national community and religious norms took priority over divergent cultural practices.
axes.counter: Recognised some religious minorities and hosted displaced people; this did not provide equal cultural autonomy or unrestricted public expression for every group.

axes.brief: National control of entry coexisted with substantial Afghan refugee protection and Islamic solidarity.
axes.counter: Asylum and humanitarian welcome are not necessarily permanent immigration rights or equal public benefit access; the modern quota questions lack direct counterparts.

axes.brief: Continued war after recovering occupied territory and supported regional revolutionary struggle.
axes.counter: Accepted UN-mediated ceasefire in 1988; this qualifies claims of rejecting diplomacy at all costs, while military defence itself is not proof of limitless aggression.

axes.brief: Independence from foreign domination and rejection of external political constraints were central.
axes.counter: Islamic international solidarity and the eventual UN ceasefire demonstrate cooperation, without establishing outside final legal authority.

axes.brief: Large-scale nationalisation and quasi-public foundations coexisted with defended private property and bazaar business.
axes.counter: Bonyads are not identical to ordinary government departments; his defence of property and suspension of land redistribution qualify blanket socialism.

axes.brief: Economic independence and strategic control favoured domestic capacity and limits on foreign ownership.
axes.counter: Imports, wartime purchases and some trade persisted; opposition to foreign domination is narrower than prohibiting all exchange.

axes.brief: War administration, controlled prices, credit direction and state sectors strongly steered allocation.
axes.counter: He mediated rival statist and private-sector tendencies rather than prescribing one fully coherent economic plan; private commerce remained.

axes.brief: Support for the oppressed and charitable/revolutionary assistance favoured material transfers.
axes.counter: Private-property protection and suspension of land redistribution limited the means; religious dues and bonyad aid differ from a universal secular tax-benefit state.

axes.brief: Islamic law, religious review and official clerical governing offices were foundational to the state.
axes.counter: Different clerics opposed aspects of his rule, but those disputes do not negate the governing doctrine of religious approval.

axes.brief: Mandatory religious dress, traditional family law and restrictive sexual norms prioritised established religious rules.
axes.counter: Women voted and took part in public life; this qualifies total exclusion while leaving traditional gender and marriage expectations strong.

axes.brief: Technical development and healthcare could be accepted within Islamic moral limits and state priorities.
axes.counter: Anti-Western cultural policy is not rejection of all technology; biomedical enhancement and irreversible-risk questions require cautious analogies rather than automatic traditionalist answers.

axes.brief: A unitary clerical-revolutionary state and suppression of separatism favoured central authority.
axes.counter: Local councils and minority communities existed but did not gain unrestricted regional sovereignty or a right to secede.

axes.brief: Religious moral formation, upbringing and education explained much conduct, alongside traditional accounts of sex differences.
axes.counter: Religious doctrine is not a documented genetics model. Estimates about stress, empathy, IQ and racial behaviour remain weak and uncertain; tradition alone does not establish racial heredity claims.
